item.title: A process-based screening framework for coastal reservoirs
item.content:encoded:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 29 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-04167-7

Reservoir geometries influence freshening while offshore wave statistics poorly proxy nearshore loads, showing that coastal reservoir suitability depends on coupled controls rather than hydrology alone, suggests a process-based screening framework applied to coastal archetypes in Taiwan.
item.dc:title: A process-based screening framework for coastal reservoirs

item.title: The finance sector should capture the full range of climate change risks
item.content:encoded:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 29 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-04160-0

Climate risk assessments used by the financial sector are often based on empirical data from recent decades that do not span the full range of possible futures. We argue that the financial sector needs to embrace risk analysis for all plausible scenarios, not just for median outcomes.
item.dc:title: The finance sector should capture the full range of climate change risks
item.dc:creator: Ajay Gambhir
Erica Thompson
Luke Kemp
David A. Stainforth
Jesse F. Abrams

item.title: Unprecedented storm impact in the Mediterranean revealed by models and seismic noise during Cyclone Harry
item.content:encoded:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 29 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-04187-3

Extratropical Cyclone Harry produced exceptional impacts in the Central Basin of the Mediterranean in January 2026 through substantial amplification of secondary microseisms, according to a synthesis of multi-disciplinary observations and modelling
item.dc:title: Unprecedented storm impact in the Mediterranean revealed by models and seismic noise during Cyclone Harry

item.title: Slow craton thickening can increase the frequency of kimberlite eruptions
item.content:encoded:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 29 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-04126-2

A gradual thickening of deep cratonic lithosphere after 1.5 Ga is consistent with, and may help explain, the long-term increase in kimberlite magmatism, according to analysis of numerical models of craton evolution and age distribution of kimberlite eruptions
item.dc:title: Slow craton thickening can increase the frequency of kimberlite eruptions
